stimuli.title: Seeds that farmers keep
stimuli.content:
In many Indian villages, farmers once kept a portion of every harvest aside as seed for the next season. Grandmothers stored grain in earthen pots sealed with mud and ash, and families exchanged seeds at weddings and fairs. Over time, this practice faded. High-yielding hybrid seeds, sold in bright packets in the market town, promised bigger harvests, and many farmers stopped saving their own.

The new seeds did raise yields, especially where water and fertiliser were plentiful. But they came with a catch. Hybrid seeds do not breed true, so a farmer who saves them finds that the next crop is weaker and uneven. He must therefore buy fresh seed every year, often on credit, and the cost rises with each season. In a dry year, when the crop fails, the farmer is left with a loan and nothing to show for it.

Community seed banks are an attempt to bring back the old habit in an organised form. A group of farmers, often led by women, collects seeds of local varieties, cleans and dries them, and stores them in a common room. A member who borrows a kilogram of seed at sowing time returns two kilograms after the harvest, so the stock grows from year to year. Records are kept in a simple register, and the seeds are tested for germination before they are lent.

The local varieties held in these banks may not match hybrids in a good year, but many of them tolerate drought, pests and poor soil far better. For a small farmer who cannot afford irrigation, a crop that yields a little less but rarely fails completely can be the wiser choice. Seed banks also preserve varieties that might otherwise disappear forever, along with the knowledge of how to grow and cook them.

Seed banks are not a rejection of modern science. Several of them work with agricultural universities to improve local varieties without losing their toughness. Their real value lies in giving farmers a choice: to buy seed when it suits them, and to rely on their own when it does not.

stimuli.title: Pumps that run on sunshine
stimuli.content:
For decades, farmers in many parts of India have watered their fields with pumps run on diesel or on grid electricity. Diesel is expensive and its price keeps changing, while the power supplied to farms often arrives for only a few hours a day, sometimes in the middle of the night. A farmer may have to walk to his field at two in the morning simply because that is when the current comes.

Solar pumps offer a way out of this daily struggle. Panels set up beside the field run the pump during daylight, when the farmer is already at work, and the fuel, sunlight, costs nothing. Once the pump is installed, the cost of running it is very low, and there is no smoke or noise. Government schemes now meet a large part of the purchase price, which has brought these pumps within the reach of many small farmers.

The benefits, however, come with a risk. Because water from a solar pump is almost free, a farmer has little reason to use it carefully. In areas where groundwater levels are already falling, free pumping could drain aquifers even faster, leaving everyone with deeper and drier wells. Experts therefore suggest that solar pumps should be combined with drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants and wastes very little.

Another idea being tried in some states is to connect solar pumps to the electricity grid. On days when the farmer does not need to irrigate, the power from his panels flows into the grid, and he is paid for it. This turns the sun into a second crop. It also gives the farmer a reason to save water, since every unit of power he does not use for pumping can be sold.

Solar pumps alone will not solve the problems of Indian agriculture. Used wisely, though, they can cut costs, free farmers from night-time irrigation and, if the incentives are right, help protect the water on which every farm depends.

stimuli.title: Forests that face the sea
stimuli.content:
Along much of India's coastline, a strip of dense, tangled forest grows where the land meets the sea. Mangroves, trees that can survive in salty water and are flooded twice a day by the tide, were long regarded as wasteland. They were cleared to make room for ports, prawn farms, salt pans and housing, and few people mourned their loss.

That view has changed, largely because of what happens when a cyclone strikes. A belt of mangroves acts like a natural breakwater. Its roots, which rise out of the mud in thick clusters, slow down the waves and trap the sediment the water carries, so that the surge reaching the villages behind is weaker and lower. Studies after major cyclones on the eastern coast found that villages sheltered by healthy mangroves generally suffered less damage than nearby villages whose forests had been cleared, although the size of the effect depended on the width of the forest and the strength of the storm.

Mangroves are also nurseries for the sea. Many fish, crabs and prawns spend their early lives among the roots, where they are protected from larger predators, before moving out into open water. Fishing communities that depend on these catches therefore have a direct stake in the forest's health. In addition, mangrove soils store large amounts of carbon, which would be released into the air if the forests were destroyed.

Restoring mangroves, however, is more difficult than simply planting saplings. Many past planting drives failed because the young trees were placed where the tide did not reach them properly, or because the species chosen did not suit the site. The most successful projects have begun by restoring the natural flow of tidal water and have involved local communities, who know the coast and have a reason to protect what grows on it.

None of this means that mangroves can replace sea walls, cyclone shelters or early-warning systems. It does mean that a forest once dismissed as useless may be among the cheapest and most lasting forms of coastal protection available, provided that it is allowed to grow where nature intended.

stimuli.title: The humble city bus
stimuli.content:
When Indian cities talk about public transport, the conversation usually turns to metro rail. Gleaming new lines are inaugurated with ceremony, and their stations become landmarks. The city bus, by comparison, receives little attention. Yet in most cities buses carry far more passengers than the metro does, and they reach neighbourhoods that no rail line will ever serve.

The neglect shows. In many cities, the number of buses has not kept pace with the population, so waits are long and vehicles are packed at peak hours. Buses share crowded roads with cars and two-wheelers and move at a crawl, which pushes anyone who can afford a vehicle to buy one. More vehicles mean more congestion, which slows the buses further, and the cycle repeats.

Breaking this cycle does not require costly technology. A dedicated lane, painted and enforced, can let a bus move faster than the cars beside it. Reliable timetables, displayed at stops and on phones, allow commuters to plan their journeys instead of waiting anxiously. Low, level boarding helps the elderly, people with disabilities and parents with small children. None of these measures costs more than a fraction of a single kilometre of metro line.

The obstacle is less money than priority. A bus lane takes road space away from private cars, and car owners, though fewer in number than bus passengers, tend to be more influential. Officials who would happily cut the ribbon on a new flyover hesitate to anger motorists by narrowing a road to make room for buses.

Cities that have made buses work, in India and abroad, share one feature: their leaders treated the bus as the backbone of the transport system rather than as a service for those with no other choice. Metro lines have their place, but a city that wants to move most of its people quickly and cheaply will have to start with the vehicle that already carries them.

stimuli.title: When the number becomes the goal
stimuli.content:
A principle familiar to economists and administrators holds that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The idea sounds paradoxical, but examples are easy to find. A hospital judged by how quickly it discharges patients may send people home before they are ready, only to see them readmitted a week later. A school rewarded for its pass rate may quietly discourage weaker students from sitting the examination. In each case the number improves while the thing it was meant to reflect stays the same or gets worse.

The reason is not that people are dishonest, though some are. It is that any single figure captures only part of what we care about. A pass rate tells us something about learning, but not everything; a discharge time tells us something about efficiency, but nothing about recovery. As long as nobody is paid or punished according to the figure, it remains a fair, if partial, signal. Once careers depend on it, effort flows towards whatever moves the number most cheaply, and the gap between the figure and the reality it was meant to track widens.

Banking offers its own illustrations. A branch given a target for opening new accounts may open thousands that are never used. A loan officer assessed on the volume of credit disbursed has little reason to dwell on whether the borrowers can repay, since the disbursement is counted today and any default arrives, if at all, years later and on someone else's watch.

None of this is an argument against measurement. An organisation that measures nothing cannot tell success from failure, and the absence of targets usually means that decisions are driven by habit or by whoever speaks loudest. The lesson is rather that numbers should be treated as instruments, not idols. Good practice includes using several indicators at once, so that gaming one shows up as a decline in another; changing targets from time to time before they can be learned and exploited; and, above all, pairing figures with judgement, exercised by people who understand the work well enough to notice when a number has stopped telling the truth.

The most dangerous moment, paradoxically, is when a measure appears to be working best. A figure that rises steadily, year after year, may be a sign of genuine progress, or a sign that people have simply become skilled at producing it.

stimuli.title: The case for keeping cash
stimuli.content:
Over the past decade, digital payments in India have grown at a pace few predicted. A vegetable seller with a printed QR code can now accept money from a stranger in seconds, and many urban consumers go days without touching a banknote. It is tempting to conclude that cash is a relic, and that the sooner it disappears the better. Such a conclusion would be premature.

Cash has qualities that digital money, for all its convenience, does not fully replicate. It works without a network, a battery or a bank account, which matters in a flood, a power failure or a remote village with patchy signal. It settles a transaction finally and instantly: once a note changes hands, there is no server to fail and no payment to reverse. And it offers a degree of privacy that many people value for reasons that have nothing to do with wrongdoing, such as an elderly widow who prefers that her relatives not see every rupee she spends.

The usual objections to cash are real but often overstated. It is true that cash can be used to evade tax and hide illegal income. Yet large-scale evasion increasingly relies on sophisticated devices, such as shell companies and inflated invoices, rather than suitcases of notes, and digital systems carry risks of their own, from fraud to outages. A payment system that depends on a single technology is efficient only for as long as that technology works.

There is also a question of fairness. Those most comfortable with digital payments tend to be young, urban and literate; those most reliant on cash tend to be older, poorer or rural. A shop that refuses notes, or a public service that can be paid for only through an app, shifts the burden of adjustment onto the people least able to bear it.

None of this is an argument for resisting digital payments, whose benefits in speed, record-keeping and reach are considerable. It is an argument for coexistence. A sensible policy would continue to encourage digital transactions while ensuring that cash remains widely accepted, easy to obtain and genuinely usable. The goal should be a society in which people choose digital payments because they are better, not because they have been left with no alternative.

stimuli.title: Gardens on the roof
stimuli.content:
In crowded Indian cities, where every square metre of land is expensive, a quiet green (1) ______ is taking place on rooftops. Families who once used their terraces only for drying clothes are now growing tomatoes, chillies, spinach and herbs in pots, old buckets and grow bags. What began as a hobby for a few retired people has (2) ______ among young professionals, many of whom say that tending plants helps them relax after a long day at a screen.

The benefits go beyond the kitchen. A terrace covered with plants absorbs some of the sun's heat, so the rooms below stay a little cooler in summer. Kitchen waste, instead of being thrown away, can be turned into compost and returned to the soil, which (3) ______ the amount of garbage a household sends to the landfill. Children who help with the watering learn where vegetables come from.

Rooftop farming does have its limits. A roof must be strong enough to bear the weight of wet soil, and water must be drained carefully so that it does not (4) ______ into the building. Beginners often lose their first plants to pests or to too much water. Most gardeners, however, learn quickly, and local groups on social media share tips, seeds and even surplus harvests.

No one expects rooftops to feed a city. But a family that grows even a part of its own vegetables learns how much effort goes into producing food and tends to waste less of it. In that sense, the small garden on the terrace may (5) ______ a lesson far larger than its size.

stimuli.title: Bring your own bottle
stimuli.content:
A walk through any city market shows how much of what we buy comes wrapped in plastic. Shampoo arrives in sachets, rice in printed bags and detergent in pouches that are used once and thrown away. Most of this packaging is (1) ______ to recycle, either because it is made of several layers fused together or because it is too small and dirty to be worth collecting. Much of it ends up in drains, rivers and landfills.

A small but growing number of shops are trying a different approach. Customers bring their own bottles and containers and refill them from large dispensers, paying only for the product, not for the packaging. Some shops weigh the empty container at the counter and (2) ______ its weight from the total, so that nobody pays for glass or steel. Others lend sturdy containers for a small deposit that is returned when the container is brought back.

The model has obvious appeal, but it faces real (3) ______. Shoppers are used to the convenience of picking a packet off the shelf, and carrying containers requires planning. Hygiene rules for loose food are strict, and dispensers must be cleaned regularly. Above all, refill shops are too few to make a difference on their own; a family that has to cross the city to refill a bottle of oil will soon (4) ______ to sachets.

Larger change will probably depend on manufacturers and big retailers. If major brands offered refill stations in ordinary supermarkets, and if rules required companies to take responsibility for the packaging they put on the market, the economics would shift quickly. Until then, the refill shop is less a solution than a (5) ______: proof that buying without throwing away is possible, and a reminder of how far we still have to go.

stimuli.title: Insuring against the sky
stimuli.content:
Every farmer knows that a single failed monsoon can **(1) wipe** out a year's income. Crop insurance is meant to soften such blows, but traditional policies have often disappointed farmers. To settle a claim, an official must visit the field and **(2) ignore** the loss, a process that is slow, costly and open to dispute. By the time the money arrives, the farmer may already have sold his cattle or borrowed at high interest to survive.

Weather-index insurance takes a different route. Instead of measuring the damage in each field, it pays out automatically when an objective index, such as the rainfall recorded at a nearby weather station, crosses an agreed limit. If rainfall during the growing season falls below the threshold, every insured farmer in the area receives a payment, whether or not an inspector has visited. Because no field visits are needed, claims can be settled quickly and administrative costs stay **(3) high**.

The approach has a weakness, which experts call basis risk: the gap between what the index records and what a particular farmer actually suffers. A weather station ten kilometres away may record adequate rain while a farmer's own field remains dry, or a crop may be destroyed by pests in a year when rainfall is perfectly normal. In such cases the farmer suffers a loss but receives nothing, and his trust in insurance is **(4) strengthened**.

Denser networks of weather stations and satellite data can narrow this gap, though they cannot close it entirely. Many specialists therefore see index insurance not as a replacement for traditional cover but as a **(5) substitute** for it: a quick, cheap first payment that keeps a household afloat, while losses that the index misses are handled in other ways.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why must a farmer who grows hybrid seeds buy fresh seed every year?

options.text: Government rules do not allow farmers to save hybrid seed.
Hybrid seed cannot be stored in earthen pots.
Seed saved from a hybrid crop gives a weaker and uneven crop.
Seed shops refuse to buy back unused hybrid seed.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says hybrid seeds 'do not breed true, so a farmer who saves them finds that the next crop is weaker and uneven. He must therefore buy fresh seed every year.'
steps: Find 'buy fresh seed every year' in paragraph 2
Read the sentence before it: the cause
Saved hybrid seed gives a weaker, uneven crop: option C
solution.why_others_wrong: No rule (A), storage problem (B) or buy-back by shops (D) is mentioned. The earthen pots belong to the old practice of saving local seed.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Seed saved from a hybrid crop gives a weaker and uneven crop.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: How, according to the passage, does the stock of a community seed bank grow from year to year?

options.text: Each member who borrows seed returns twice the quantity after the harvest.
The government adds fresh seed to the bank every season.
Agricultural universities donate hybrid seed to the bank.
Members buy seed in the market town and deposit it in the bank.

solution.concept: Locating a stated mechanism
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says a member who borrows a kilogram at sowing time 'returns two kilograms after the harvest, so the stock grows from year to year'.
steps: Mechanism: borrow one kilogram, return two
solution.why_others_wrong: Government additions (B) are not mentioned. The universities help improve local varieties; they do not donate hybrid seed (C). Buying seed in the market (D) is what seed banks help farmers avoid.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Each member who borrows seed returns twice the quantity after the harvest.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as part of the way a seed bank works?

options.text: Seeds are cleaned and dried before storage.
Members pay a yearly fee in cash to the group.
Records are kept in a simple register.
Seeds are tested for germination before they are lent.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 mentions cleaning and drying (A), a simple register (C) and germination tests (D). No cash fee is mentioned; members repay in seed, not money.
steps: Paragraph 3: cleans and dries (A), register (C), germination test (D)
Repayment is in seed: two kilograms for one
A cash fee is not mentioned: B
solution.why_others_wrong: A, C and D are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the 'NOT mentioned' answer.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Members pay a yearly fee in cash to the group.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, might a small farmer without irrigation prefer local varieties to hybrids?

options.text: Local varieties always give higher yields than hybrids.
Local varieties are sold at a higher price in the market town.
Hybrid seeds cannot be grown without the help of a university.
Local varieties yield a little less but rarely fail completely in hard conditions.

solution.concept: Inference: weighing yield against risk
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says local varieties 'may not match hybrids in a good year' but tolerate drought, pests and poor soil. For a farmer without irrigation, a crop that 'rarely fails completely can be the wiser choice'.
steps: Farmer's situation: no irrigation, so drought is a real risk
Local varieties: slightly lower yield, much lower risk of total failure
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the passage, which admits local varieties may yield less in a good year. Market prices (B) are not discussed. C is not stated; universities work with seed banks but hybrids do not need them.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Local varieties yield a little less but rarely fail completely in hard conditions.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Why Hybrid Seeds Should Be Banned
Seed Banks: Giving Farmers a Choice

solution.concept: A title must cover the main idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage traces the decline of seed saving, the drawbacks of relying only on bought hybrid seed, how community seed banks work and why they matter. Its last sentence names their value: giving farmers a choice.
steps: Paras 1–2: old habit lost; problems with depending on hybrids
Paras 3–4: how seed banks work and why local varieties help
Para 5: seed banks give farmers a choice: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A goes too far: the passage says seed banks are 'not a rejection of modern science'. B is far wider than the passage. C picks up one detail from the first paragraph.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Seed Banks: Giving Farmers a Choice

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why might a farmer have to go to his field at two in the morning?

options.text: Electricity for farms is often supplied only at certain hours, sometimes at night.
Solar panels work best before sunrise.
Drip irrigation must be done when it is cool.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says farm power 'often arrives for only a few hours a day, sometimes in the middle of the night', so the farmer goes at two in the morning 'because that is when the current comes'.
steps: Find 'two in the morning' in paragraph 1
Reason: that is when the current comes
solution.why_others_wrong: A: the passage says diesel is expensive and its price keeps changing, not that it is cheaper at night. C is absurd: solar panels need daylight. D is not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Electricity for farms is often supplied only at certain hours, sometimes at night.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What risk of solar pumps does the passage point out?

options.text: The panels are easily stolen from the fields.
The pumps make a great deal of noise.
Government schemes may stop paying for them.
Because pumping costs almost nothing, farmers may overuse groundwater.

solution.concept: Locating a stated drawback
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that because water from a solar pump is almost free, a farmer has little reason to use it carefully, and free pumping could drain aquifers faster.
solution.why_others_wrong: Theft (A) and the end of government schemes (C) are not mentioned. B contradicts paragraph 2, which says the pumps make no smoke or noise.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Because pumping costs almost nothing, farmers may overuse groundwater.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: How, according to the passage, does connecting solar pumps to the grid encourage farmers to save water?

options.text: Power the farmer does not use for pumping can be sold, so saving water earns him money.
The grid company limits the amount of water each farmer may pump.
Grid-connected pumps cannot run for more than a few hours a day.
Farmers who join the grid must also install drip irrigation.

solution.concept: Inference: following an incentive
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the farmer is paid for the power his panels send to the grid, and 'every unit of power he does not use for pumping can be sold'. Pumping less water therefore earns him more.
steps: Grid link: unused solar power is sold
Less pumping → more power to sell → more income
So the farmer gains by saving water: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D describe limits or conditions that the passage never mentions. The incentive works through payment, not through rules.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Power the farmer does not use for pumping can be sold, so saving water earns him money.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'drain' as used in the passage ('free pumping could drain aquifers even faster')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: drain = use up, empty
solution.explanation: The sentence says overuse could leave 'deeper and drier wells'. Pumping out underground water faster than it is replaced empties the aquifers.
steps: So 'drain' means empty or use up
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fill' is the opposite. 'Clean' and 'measure' do not explain why wells would become deeper and drier.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how does a belt of mangroves reduce the damage caused by a cyclone?

options.text: It warns villagers in advance that a storm is approaching.
It stores carbon that would otherwise make storms stronger.
Its roots slow the waves and trap sediment, so the surge reaching villages is weaker and lower.
It provides timber for building stronger houses.

solution.concept: Locating a stated mechanism
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the roots 'slow down the waves and trap the sediment the water carries, so that the surge reaching the villages behind is weaker and lower'.
steps: Mechanism: roots slow waves and trap sediment
solution.why_others_wrong: A: early warning is something mangroves cannot replace, according to the last paragraph. B: carbon storage is a separate benefit and is not linked to storm strength. D: timber is never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Its roots slow the waves and trap sediment, so the surge reaching villages is weaker and lower.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The clause 'although the size of the effect depended on the width of the forest and the strength of the storm' suggests that

options.text: the protection mangroves give is real but varies, and is not unlimited
mangroves give no protection against strong storms
only very wide forests should be protected
the studies after the cyclones were unreliable

solution.concept: Inference: the purpose of a qualifying clause
solution.explanation: The main clause reports a benefit (less damage behind healthy mangroves); the 'although' clause qualifies it: how much protection a forest gives depends on its width and the storm's strength. The benefit is real but varies.
steps: Main claim: mangrove villages generally suffered less damage
'although' adds a limit, not a denial
So the protection is real but variable: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B turns a limit into a denial and contradicts 'generally suffered less damage'. C is a policy the passage never proposes. D questions the studies, which the author relies on.
solution.final_answer: Option A: the protection mangroves give is real but varies, and is not unlimited

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a benefit of mangroves?

options.text: Sheltering young fish, crabs and prawns
Reducing the force of storm surges

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question
solution.explanation: The passage names three benefits: protection from surges (paragraph 2), nurseries for marine life and carbon storage (paragraph 3). Housing appears only as one of the reasons mangroves were cleared, not as a benefit.
steps: Para 3: young fish, crabs, prawns (A); carbon (B)
Housing is a reason for clearing them, not a benefit: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each stated as benefits, so none of them is the 'NOT mentioned' answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Providing timber for coastal housing

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What can be inferred from the passage about successful mangrove restoration?

options.text: It depends mainly on planting as many saplings as possible.
It depends on suitable tidal conditions and the involvement of local people more than on the number of saplings.
It can be achieved quickly by choosing a single fast-growing species everywhere.
It is no longer necessary, because sea walls give better protection.

solution.concept: Inference from contrasting failures and successes
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 says past drives failed when trees were planted where the tide did not reach them or the wrong species was chosen, while the best projects restored tidal flow and involved local communities. Success therefore turns on site conditions and people, not on sapling numbers.
steps: Failures: wrong place for the tide, wrong species
Successes: tidal flow restored, local people involved
Conclusion: conditions and community matter more than numbers: B
solution.why_others_wrong: A is what the passage says is not enough ('more difficult than simply planting saplings'). C contradicts the failure caused by species that did not suit the site. D contradicts the last paragraph, which values mangroves alongside sea walls.
solution.final_answer: Option B: It depends on suitable tidal conditions and the involvement of local people more than on the number of saplings.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards mangroves as a form of coastal protection?

solution.concept: Tone: look for praise together with limits
solution.explanation: The author praises mangroves as among the cheapest and most lasting forms of protection, but also says they cannot replace sea walls or early warnings, that their effect varies and that restoration is hard. That is appreciation with clear limits.
steps: Limits: effect varies; cannot replace sea walls; restoration difficult
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Dismissive' is the old view the author rejects. 'Uncritically enthusiastic' ignores the stated limits. 'Indifferent' does not fit a passage that argues a case.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, how do buses compare with the metro in most Indian cities?

options.text: Buses carry far more passengers and reach neighbourhoods that rail lines will never serve.
Buses are faster than the metro at peak hours.
Buses receive more public attention than the metro.
Buses cost more to run per kilometre than the metro.

solution.concept: Locating a stated comparison
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 says that 'in most cities buses carry far more passengers than the metro does, and they reach neighbourhoods that no rail line will ever serve'.
steps: Find the comparison in paragraph 1 ('Yet in most cities ...')
Two points: more passengers, wider reach
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts paragraph 2: buses 'move at a crawl'. C reverses paragraph 1: buses receive 'little attention'. D: the passage compares the cost of bus measures with metro construction, not running costs per kilometre.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Buses carry far more passengers and reach neighbourhoods that rail lines will never serve.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does 'the cycle' in 'and the cycle repeats' (paragraph 2) refer to?

options.text: The daily timetable of buses on a route
The rise and fall of fares every year
Commuters switching between buses and bicycles
Slow buses push people to buy vehicles, which adds to congestion and slows buses further

solution.concept: Inference: identify what a summarising phrase refers to
solution.explanation: The sentences before it describe a loop: buses crawl → people who can afford it buy vehicles → more vehicles mean more congestion → buses slow down further. 'The cycle' is this self-reinforcing loop.
steps: Trace paragraph 2: slow buses → more private vehicles
More vehicles → more congestion → slower buses
The loop returns to its start: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C name cycles the paragraph never describes; fares and bicycles are not mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Slow buses push people to buy vehicles, which adds to congestion and slows buses further

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the author, what is the main obstacle to improving bus services?

options.text: The high cost of the technology needed
Officials' reluctance to take road space from car owners, who are more influential
A shortage of trained bus drivers

solution.concept: Inference: the author's stated main obstacle
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 begins: 'The obstacle is less money than priority.' Bus lanes take space from cars, and car owners are more influential, so officials hesitate to anger them.
steps: Key sentence: 'The obstacle is less money than priority'
Bus lanes take road space from cars
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts paragraph 3, which says the measures do not need costly technology. C is never mentioned. D contradicts paragraph 3, which presents reliable timetables as a help to commuters.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Officials' reluctance to take road space from car owners, who are more influential

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'backbone' as used in the passage ('treated the bus as the backbone of the transport system')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: figurative 'backbone'
solution.explanation: The backbone is the part that supports everything else. Treating the bus as the backbone, 'rather than as a service for those with no other choice', means treating it as the main support of the system: its mainstay.
steps: Contrast: backbone vs 'a service for those with no other choice'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Afterthought' is close to the opposite. 'Rival' and 'luxury' do not fit a system's central support.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The examples of the hospital and the school in the first paragraph are used mainly to show that

options.text: a figure can improve even while the outcome it is meant to reflect stays the same or worsens
hospitals and schools are run less efficiently than banks
most administrators deliberately falsify their records
discharge times and pass rates should never be measured

solution.concept: Inference: the function of examples
solution.explanation: Both examples end the same way: the number (discharge speed, pass rate) improves, but the real goal (recovery, learning) does not. The paragraph's last sentence states this directly.
steps: School: higher pass rate, but weaker students kept out
Shared point (last sentence of para 1): A
solution.why_others_wrong: B makes a comparison the passage never makes. C contradicts paragraph 2: 'The reason is not that people are dishonest'. D contradicts paragraph 4: 'None of this is an argument against measurement'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: a figure can improve even while the outcome it is meant to reflect stays the same or worsens

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why does a figure become less reliable once careers depend on it?

options.text: People stop recording it accurately because it is tedious to collect.
It becomes too expensive for the organisation to measure.
Dishonest people are attracted to jobs that carry targets.
Effort shifts to whatever moves the figure most cheaply, so the figure drifts away from the reality it tracked.

solution.concept: Locating the author's explanation
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Once careers depend on it, effort flows towards whatever moves the number most cheaply, and the gap between the figure and the reality it was meant to track widens.'
steps: Find 'Once careers depend on it' in paragraph 2
Mechanism: effort goes to the cheapest way of moving the number
Result: figure and reality drift apart: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B give reasons the passage never mentions. C contradicts the author, who says the reason is 'not that people are dishonest'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Effort shifts to whatever moves the figure most cheaply, so the figure drifts away from the reality it tracked.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The phrase 'on someone else's watch', used about a loan officer, suggests that

options.text: loan officers are usually transferred before they are trained
defaults are recorded by a different department of the bank
a bad loan's cost is likely to surface after the officer who made it has moved on, so he does not bear it
borrowers deliberately delay repayment until the officer retires

solution.concept: Inference: meaning of an idiom in context
solution.explanation: 'On someone else's watch' means during another person's period of responsibility. The disbursement is credited to the officer today, while any default comes years later, when someone else is in charge, so the officer has little reason to worry about repayment.
steps: Idiom: 'on X's watch' = while X is responsible
Disbursement counted now; default arrives later
So the cost falls on a successor: C
solution.why_others_wrong: A and D invent motives and events. B takes 'someone else' too literally; the point is about timing and responsibility, not departments.
solution.final_answer: Option C: a bad loan's cost is likely to surface after the officer who made it has moved on, so he does not bear it

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: With which of the following statements would the author most likely agree?

options.text: Using several indicators together, interpreted by people who understand the work, reduces the risk of gaming.
Organisations would be better off without any targets at all.
A figure that rises steadily every year can safely be taken as proof of progress.
Gaming of targets happens mainly because employees are dishonest.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's recommendations
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 recommends using several indicators at once, 'so that gaming one shows up as a decline in another', and pairing figures with the judgement of people who understand the work. Option A combines the two.
steps: Para 4 lists remedies: several indicators; changing targets; judgement
Option A restates two of them
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts 'None of this is an argument against measurement'. C contradicts the last paragraph, which warns that a steadily rising figure may reflect skill at producing it. D contradicts 'The reason is not that people are dishonest'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Using several indicators together, interpreted by people who understand the work, reduces the risk of gaming.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the sentence 'numbers should be treated as instruments, not idols', the word 'idols' most nearly means

options.text: tools to be used with care

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: figurative 'idols' contrasted with 'instruments'
solution.explanation: An instrument is a tool we use and judge; an idol is something worshipped without question. The author warns against treating numbers as beyond question.
steps: Figurative meaning: something revered without question: D
solution.why_others_wrong: A describes 'instruments', the opposite side of the contrast. B and C do not capture the sense of uncritical devotion.
solution.final_answer: Option D: objects of unquestioning reverence

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards numerical targets?

options.text: Wholly opposed to the use of targets
Supportive of measurement but wary of treating any single figure as the goal
Indifferent to how organisations are assessed

solution.concept: Tone: a balanced position stated in the fourth paragraph
solution.explanation: The author defends measurement ('An organisation that measures nothing cannot tell success from failure') while warning, throughout, against making one figure the goal. That is support with caution.
steps: For measurement: para 4, first two sentences
solution.why_others_wrong: A ignores the defence of measurement. B ignores the passage's many warnings. D does not fit a passage that argues a definite case.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Supportive of measurement but wary of treating any single figure as the goal

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a quality of cash?

options.text: It works without a network, a battery or a bank account.
It settles a transaction finally and instantly.
It offers a degree of privacy.
It earns interest for as long as it is held.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists three qualities: it works without network, battery or account (A); it settles finally and instantly (B); it offers privacy (C). Earning interest is not mentioned, and notes held as cash earn none.
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are all stated in paragraph 2, so none of them can be the 'NOT mentioned' answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It earns interest for as long as it is held.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: The statement 'A payment system that depends on a single technology is efficient only for as long as that technology works' implies that

options.text: keeping more than one means of payment makes the system more resilient to failures
digital payments are less efficient than cash in normal times
technology should be removed from payment systems altogether
outages in digital payment systems happen every day

solution.concept: Inference: unstated implication of a general statement
solution.explanation: If a system that relies on one technology fails whenever that technology fails, then keeping an alternative, such as cash, protects the system during outages. The statement argues for having more than one way to pay.
steps: Fits the passage's call for coexistence: A
solution.why_others_wrong: B contradicts the passage, which praises the speed of digital payments. C goes far beyond it; the author wants coexistence, not removal. D exaggerates; the passage mentions outages only as one risk.
solution.final_answer: Option A: keeping more than one means of payment makes the system more resilient to failures

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: How does the author deal with the argument that cash helps people evade tax?

options.text: The author rejects it as entirely false.
The author treats it as a decisive reason to abolish cash.
The author accepts that it has some truth but argues that it is often overstated.
The author does not mention it at all.

solution.concept: Inference: the author's treatment of a counter-argument
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins 'The usual objections to cash are real but often overstated', concedes 'It is true that cash can be used to evade tax', and then argues that large-scale evasion increasingly uses other devices.
steps: Limitation: 'often overstated'; evasion uses shell companies
solution.why_others_wrong: A ignores the concession. B is the opposite of the author's conclusion. D is wrong: paragraph 3 discusses the point directly.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The author accepts that it has some truth but argues that it is often overstated.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why can a policy that pushes everyone towards digital payments be unfair?

options.text: It raises the prices that urban consumers pay.
It harms shopkeepers more than it harms customers.
Young people find digital payments difficult to use.
It puts the burden of adjusting on older, poorer and rural people, who rely most on cash.

solution.concept: Inference: following the fairness argument
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 contrasts the young, urban and literate, who are comfortable with digital payments, with the older, poorer or rural, who rely on cash. Refusing cash 'shifts the burden of adjustment onto the people least able to bear it'.
steps: Para 4: two groups with different comfort levels
Cash-only refusals burden the second group
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B are not mentioned. C reverses the passage, which says the young are the most comfortable with digital payments.
solution.final_answer: Option D: It puts the burden of adjusting on older, poorer and rural people, who rely most on cash.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.text: Cash and Digital Payments: The Case for Coexistence
Why Cash Must Replace Digital Payments
The History of the Banknote in India
How QR Codes Changed Street Vending

solution.concept: A title must match the author's conclusion and cover the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage defends the qualities of cash, weighs the objections and ends: 'It is an argument for coexistence.' Option A captures both the topic and the conclusion.
steps: Final paragraph: not against digital payments; 'an argument for coexistence'
Body: the qualities of cash, objections, fairness
solution.why_others_wrong: B reverses the author's position, which welcomes digital payments. C is not discussed. D picks up one example from the first paragraph.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Cash and Digital Payments: The Case for Coexistence

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the paragraph describes a spreading new trend
solution.explanation: The paragraph describes many families turning their terraces into gardens. A widespread change that happens without noise is a 'quiet green revolution'.
steps: The sentences after the blank describe a growing change
'quiet ... revolution' = a big change without fuss
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Silence' and 'dispute' do not describe a change that is 'taking place'. 'Decline' contradicts the growth of the hobby described next.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: phrasal verb 'catch on' = become popular
solution.explanation: A hobby that began with a few retired people and is now taken up by young professionals has become popular among them: it has 'caught on'.
steps: Contrast: began with a few retired people → now young professionals
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Given up' and 'died out' mean the opposite. 'Set off' means started a journey or triggered something and does not fit 'among young professionals'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: effect of composting on household garbage
solution.explanation: Waste that is composted instead of thrown away no longer goes to the landfill, so composting reduces the amount of garbage a household sends there.
steps: 'instead of being thrown away' → less waste leaves the house
So the amount sent to landfill falls
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Increases' and 'doubles' reverse the effect. 'Hides' suggests the garbage still exists but is concealed, which is not what composting does.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: verb for water slowly passing through a surface
solution.explanation: Badly drained water on a roof can slowly pass through cracks into the rooms below. The verb for this is 'seep'.
steps: Danger: it passes slowly through into the building
solution.why_others_wrong: Water does not 'fly', 'climb' or 'jump' into a building; none of these describes slow leakage.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'carry a lesson' = contain or convey a lesson
solution.explanation: The last paragraph says a family learns about the effort behind food and wastes less. The small garden therefore carries (conveys) a lesson larger than itself.
steps: Preceding sentence: the family learns something important
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lose', 'deny' and 'waste' a lesson all mean the lesson is missed, which contradicts the sentence before it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the 'because' clauses explain the blank
solution.explanation: The packaging is hard to recycle 'because it is made of several layers fused together or because it is too small and dirty to be worth collecting'. Both reasons are problems, so 'difficult' fits.
steps: Read the 'either because ... or because' reasons
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Easy' and 'cheap' contradict the reasons and the next sentence (it ends up in drains and rivers). 'Designed to recycle' is ungrammatical here and would also contradict the reasons.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'from the total' with the purpose 'so that nobody pays for glass or steel'
solution.explanation: To make sure customers do not pay for their own container, the shop takes its weight away from the total: it deducts the weight.
steps: Purpose: nobody pays for the container
So its weight must be taken off the total
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Add' would make customers pay for the container. 'Measure' and 'hide' do not go with 'from the total' and do not achieve the stated purpose.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'but' introduces the difficulties listed next
solution.explanation: After 'The model has obvious appeal, but ...', the paragraph lists problems: habits of convenience, strict hygiene rules and too few shops. These are obstacles.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rewards' and 'profits' are positives and remove the contrast. 'Faces real customers' does not introduce the list of difficulties that follows.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'revert to' = go back to an earlier habit
solution.explanation: A family that finds refilling too inconvenient will go back to its old habit of buying sachets. 'Revert to' means return to a previous state or practice.
steps: Situation: refilling means crossing the city
Likely result: going back to sachets
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Refer to', 'react to' and 'relate to' are all grammatical with 'to' but do not mean going back to an old habit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the words after the colon define the blank
solution.explanation: After the colon, the refill shop is called 'proof that buying without throwing away is possible'. Something that proves a thing possible is a demonstration.
steps: Read after the colon: 'proof that ... is possible'
Proof that something can be done = a demonstration
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Failure' and 'nuisance' contradict 'proof that ... is possible'. A 'secret' cannot serve as public proof or a reminder.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'a single failed monsoon can wipe out a year's income'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the phrasal verb 'wipe out' = destroy completely
solution.explanation: 'Wipe out' means destroy or remove completely, and a failed monsoon can destroy a whole year's income. The word is correct as it stands.
steps: Meaning needed: completely destroy the year's income
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Clear out', 'rub out' and 'sweep out' mean emptying or erasing something physically and do not describe the loss of income.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'an official must visit the field and ignore the loss, a process that is slow, costly and open to dispute'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: what an official visits a field to do
solution.explanation: To settle a claim, the official must measure, or assess, the loss. An official who 'ignores' the loss could not settle a claim, and the next paragraph contrasts this with 'measuring the damage in each field'.
steps: Purpose of the visit: to settle a claim
That requires judging the size of the loss
Next paragraph confirms: 'measuring the damage': replace with 'assess'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Overlook' repeats the error of 'ignore'. 'Inflate' means exaggerate, which is not the official's task. 'Ignore' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'Because no field visits are needed, claims can be settled quickly and administrative costs stay high'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: follow the cause ('Because no field visits are needed')
solution.explanation: Field visits make traditional claims 'slow, costly'. Removing them makes settlement quick and keeps administrative costs low. 'High' contradicts the cause given in the same sentence.
steps: Effects: quick settlement and smaller costs
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rising' and 'heavy' repeat the error of 'high'. 'High' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'the farmer suffers a loss but receives nothing, and his trust in insurance is strengthened'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: effect of an unpaid loss on trust
solution.explanation: A farmer who suffers a loss and receives no payment loses faith in insurance. His trust is weakened, not strengthened.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Deepened' and 'confirmed' repeat the error by making trust grow. 'Strengthened' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'not as a replacement for traditional cover but as a substitute for it'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'not X but Y' needs Y to differ from X; complement vs compliment
solution.explanation: 'Not as a replacement ... but as a substitute' says the same thing twice, so 'substitute' is wrong. The colon explains that index insurance gives a quick first payment while other losses are 'handled in other ways': it works alongside traditional cover, completing it. That is a 'complement' (something that completes).
steps: 'not a replacement but a ___' → the blank must mean something other than a replacement
After the colon: index insurance plus other cover together
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Alternative' means the same as replacement, like 'substitute'. 'Compliment' means an expression of praise, a different word. 'Substitute' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply. (The preposition 'for it' would become 'to it' with 'complement'.)

questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The bank sent me (A) / all the informations (B) / I needed to open an account. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: I needed to open an account.

solution.concept: 'Information' is uncountable and has no plural form
solution.explanation: 'Information' is an uncountable noun, so it never takes '-s': 'all the information I needed'.
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject, verb and indirect object. Part C is a correct relative clause. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The farmer told us (A) / that his cattle (B) / was grazing near the river. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Cattle' is a plural noun and takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'Cattle' has no singular form and is always plural: 'his cattle were grazing near the river'.
steps: 'was grazing' → 'were grazing': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct past-tense reporting clause. Part B correctly introduces the clause. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: was grazing near the river.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Please return back (A) / the signed form (B) / by Friday. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Redundancy: 'return' already means 'give or come back'
solution.explanation: 'Return' means 'give back', so 'return back' says the same thing twice. The correct form is 'Please return the signed form by Friday.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct object and part C a correct time phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
During the year-end closing, (A) / she is used (B) / to work late hours. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Be/get used to' + gerund ('to' is a preposition here)
solution.explanation: In 'be used to' (be accustomed to), 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an -ing form: 'she is used to working late hours'. ('Used to work', with no 'be', means a past habit that has stopped.)
steps: Expression: 'be used to' = be accustomed to
'to work' → 'to working': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time phrase. Part B ('is used') is a correct form of the expression. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: to work late hours.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The bank has revised its rates (A) / on all fixed deposits (B) / with effect from Monday. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The bank has revised its rates

solution.concept: Checking a correct sentence part by part
solution.explanation: The sentence is correct. 'Its' is the possessive (no apostrophe), the present perfect 'has revised' suits a recent change with a present result, 'rates on deposits' is the standard collocation and 'with effect from' is the correct fixed phrase.
steps: Part A: 'has revised its rates': correct possessive and tense
Part B: 'rates on all fixed deposits': correct
Part C: 'with effect from Monday': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of parts A, B and C is correct, as shown in the steps, so none of them is the answer.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The canteen orders three dozens (A) / bananas every morning (B) / for the staff. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Dozen' after a number takes no '-s'
solution.explanation: When 'dozen' follows a number, it stays singular: 'three dozen bananas'. ('Dozens of' is used only without a number, meaning 'many'.)
steps: 'three dozens' → 'three dozen': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('bananas every morning') and part C ('for the staff') are correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The canteen orders three dozens

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The cash van (A) / reached to the branch (B) / just after ten. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Reach' (arrive at) takes a direct object, with no 'to'
solution.explanation: 'Reach' meaning 'arrive at' is transitive: 'The cash van reached the branch just after ten.' 'Reached to' is wrong.
steps: It takes a direct object without a preposition
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and part C a correct time phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: reached to the branch

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The salary of a clerk (A) / is lower than (B) / a branch manager. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Compare like with like: salary with salary, not salary with a person
solution.explanation: The sentence compares a clerk's salary with a branch manager (a person). It should compare salary with salary: 'lower than that of a branch manager' (or 'than a branch manager's').
steps: What is being compared? 'The salary of a clerk'
It must be compared with another salary
'than a branch manager' → 'than that of a branch manager': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and part B a correct comparative. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Prices of vegetables (A) / have raised sharply (B) / since the floods. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Rise (intransitive: rise – rose – risen) vs raise (transitive: raise – raised – raised)
solution.explanation: Prices go up by themselves; nothing is being lifted by someone. The intransitive verb 'rise' is needed: 'Prices have risen sharply.'
steps: Is there an object after the verb? No
Past participle of 'rise' is 'risen': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct plural subject and part C a correct 'since' phrase with the present perfect. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Beside his salary, (A) / he earns a small income (B) / from his farm. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Besides (in addition to) vs beside (next to)
solution.explanation: The meaning is 'in addition to his salary', which needs 'Besides'. 'Beside' means 'next to', which makes no sense with a salary.
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct main clause and part C a correct source phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
By evening the cashier was (A) / so tired to count (B) / the remaining notes. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Too + adjective + to-infinitive' vs 'so + adjective + that-clause'
solution.explanation: 'So tired to count' mixes two patterns. The correct forms are 'too tired to count the remaining notes' or 'so tired that he could not count the remaining notes'.
steps: 'so tired to count' mixes them: error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct clause opening and part C a correct object. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: so tired to count

Although the loan was approved in March, but (A) / the money was released (B) / only in June. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Although the loan was approved in March, but

solution.concept: 'Although' and 'but' are not used together in one sentence
solution.explanation: 'Although' already links the two clauses with a contrast, so adding 'but' is a double connector. Correct: 'Although the loan was approved in March, the money was released only in June' (or 'The loan was approved in March, but ...'). Both connectors sit in part A.
steps: Part A contains two connectors: 'Although' and 'but'
Drop one of them: error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct passive verb phrase and part C a correct time phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Although the loan was approved in March, but

The officer explained me (A) / the terms of the loan (B) / in simple words. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Explain something to someone' (not 'explain someone something')
solution.explanation: 'Explain' cannot take the person as a direct object. The correct form is 'The officer explained the terms of the loan to me in simple words.'
steps: 'explained me' is wrong: error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Parts B and C are correct as phrases; the error lies in the verb pattern in A. So 'No error' is wrong.
