Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
When have you submitted (A) / the documents for (B) / the home loan? (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'When' asks about a definite past time, so it takes the simple past, not the present perfect
solution.explanation: A question with 'When' points to a specific time in the past, which needs the simple past: 'When did you submit the documents for the home loan?'
steps: 'When have you submitted' → 'When did you submit': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Parts B and C are correct. The error is the tense in A, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: When have you submitted

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
I will call you (A) / as soon as the cheque (B) / will be cleared. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Time clauses ('as soon as', 'when', 'after') use the present tense for a future meaning
solution.explanation: In a time clause introduced by 'as soon as', the present tense is used even for a future event: 'as soon as the cheque is cleared'. 'Will' belongs only in the main clause.
steps: Main clause: 'I will call you' (future, correct)
Time clause with 'as soon as' → present tense
'will be cleared' → 'is cleared': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'will' in the main clause and part B correctly introduces the time clause. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The committee's recommendations (A) / have been accepted (B) / by the board in full. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Checking a correct sentence: plural subject, present perfect passive, agent
solution.explanation: The sentence is correct. The subject 'recommendations' is plural, so 'have been accepted' agrees; the possessive 'committee's' is correctly formed; and 'by the board in full' is a correct agent phrase.
steps: Part B: plural verb 'have been accepted': agrees
Part C: agent and adverbial: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of parts A, B and C is correct, as shown in the steps, so none of them is the answer.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The committee recommended (A) / simplifying the forms, cutting the fees (B) / and that branches should open on Sundays. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: simplifying the forms, cutting the fees
and that branches should open on Sundays.

solution.concept: Parallel structure: items in a list must have the same grammatical form
solution.explanation: The list after 'recommended' begins with two gerund phrases ('simplifying ...', 'cutting ...'), so the third item must also be a gerund phrase: 'and opening branches on Sundays'. Switching to a 'that' clause breaks the parallelism.
steps: Item 3: 'that branches should open' (clause): not parallel, error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and verb, and part B lists two correct parallel gerunds. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: and that branches should open on Sundays.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Of the two brothers who run the firm, (A) / Arun, who is elder than Vikram, (B) / looks after the accounts. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Of the two brothers who run the firm,
Arun, who is elder than Vikram,

solution.concept: 'Elder' is not followed by 'than'; use 'older than'
solution.explanation: 'Elder' is used before a noun ('my elder brother') or as 'the elder of the two', but not with 'than'. The comparative with 'than' is 'older': 'Arun, who is older than Vikram, ...'.
steps: 'elder than' → 'older than': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct introductory phrase and part C a correct main verb that agrees with 'Arun'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Arun, who is elder than Vikram,

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The recovery team has worked (A) / very hardly this quarter (B) / to bring down overdue loans. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Hard (adverb: with great effort) vs hardly (adverb: almost not)
solution.explanation: 'Hard' is itself an adverb meaning 'with great effort'. 'Hardly' means 'almost not', so 'worked very hardly' would say the team barely worked, which contradicts the purpose clause. Correct: 'has worked very hard this quarter'.
steps: Intended meaning: worked with great effort
'very hardly' → 'very hard': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject and present perfect, and part C a correct purpose clause. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: very hardly this quarter

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
So severe was the drought (A) / that the bank rescheduled (B) / all crop loans in the district. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: all crop loans in the district.

solution.concept: Inversion after 'So + adjective' at the start of a sentence
solution.explanation: When 'So + adjective' opens a sentence, the verb comes before the subject: 'So severe was the drought that ...'. The result clause 'that the bank rescheduled all crop loans' is also correct. The sentence has no error.
steps: Part A: 'So severe was the drought': correct inversion
Part B: 'that' introduces the result; past tense matches
Part C: correct object and place phrase
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of parts A, B and C is correct, as shown in the steps, so none of them is the answer. The inversion in A is required, not an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
A great deal of applications (A) / were rejected (B) / because of missing documents. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'A great deal of' goes with uncountable nouns; countable plurals take 'a great many' or 'a large number of'
solution.explanation: 'Applications' is a countable plural, so 'a great deal of applications' is wrong. Correct: 'A great many applications were rejected' or 'A large number of applications were rejected'.
steps: 'A great deal of' is only for uncountable nouns (a great deal of time)
Use 'A great many' / 'A large number of': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('were rejected') correctly agrees with the plural 'applications'. Part C is a correct reason phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A great deal of applications

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
She **is working in this branch since** 2019.

options.text: has been working in this branch since
was working in this branch since
is working in this branch from

solution.concept: Present perfect continuous for an action that began in the past and continues now ('since + point of time')
solution.explanation: The work began in 2019 and still continues. An action running from a past point up to now takes the present perfect continuous: 'She has been working in this branch since 2019.'
steps: Time marker: 'since 2019' (starting point in the past)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was working' suggests the work is over. 'Is working ... from' keeps the wrong present continuous. The original uses the present continuous with 'since', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: has been working in this branch since

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
**Let he** handle the cash counter today.

solution.concept: 'Let' is followed by an object pronoun and a bare infinitive
solution.explanation: 'Let' takes an object, so the pronoun must be in the object form: 'Let him handle the cash counter today.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'His' is a possessive and 'Let he will' adds a modal after 'let'; both are ungrammatical. The original uses the subject form 'he', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The heritage museum next to the head office **is worth to visit** on a weekend.

solution.concept: 'Worth' + gerund (never 'worth to' + verb)
solution.explanation: The adjective 'worth' is followed by an -ing form: 'The museum is worth visiting.' 'Worth to visit' is not used.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Worthy to visiting' mixes 'worthy' with a preposition and a gerund. 'Worth for visiting' adds an unnecessary preposition. The to-infinitive in the original is wrong after 'worth', so 'No improvement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
During the training, the new recruits **were made to sit** through a three-hour session on fraud prevention.

solution.concept: Causative 'make': bare infinitive in the active, to-infinitive in the passive
solution.explanation: In the active, 'make' takes a bare infinitive ('They made the recruits sit'). In the passive, 'to' returns: 'The recruits were made to sit'. The sentence is already correct.
steps: Passive of 'make someone do' → 'be made to do'
'were made to sit' is correct: no improvement
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Were made sit' drops the 'to' that the passive needs. 'Were made sitting' uses the wrong verb form. 'Had made to sit' turns the passive into an incorrect active form with no object.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The bank promised to **look after** the customer's complaint and reply within a week.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'look': look into = investigate
solution.explanation: A complaint is investigated before the bank replies. 'Look into' means investigate; 'look after' means take care of a person or thing.
steps: Context: a complaint to be examined before replying
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Look up' means search for information in a book or list. 'Look down on' means regard as inferior. The original 'look after' (take care of) does not suit a complaint, so 'No replacement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
A few large defaults **accounted by** most of the bank's losses last year.

solution.concept: 'Account for' = make up, form (a proportion of)
solution.explanation: The defaults made up most of the losses. The phrasal verb is 'account for': 'A few large defaults accounted for most of the bank's losses.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Accounted to' means reported to someone. 'Were accounted' is an incomplete passive that makes no sense here. 'Accounted by' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
When his father retired, Ravi **took after** the family's grain business.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'take': take over = assume control of
solution.explanation: When the father retired, Ravi assumed control of the business: he 'took over' the family's grain business. 'Take after' means to resemble a parent.
steps: Context: father retires; son steps in
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Took up with' means began to associate with someone. 'Took off' means departed or became successful and cannot take this object. 'Took after' (resembled) is wrong here, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Despite heavy publicity, the new deposit scheme **fell short of** the bank's targets.

solution.concept: Fixed expression: 'fall short of' = fail to reach
solution.explanation: 'Fall short of a target' means fail to reach it, which fits 'Despite heavy publicity'. The phrase is already correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fell short from' and 'fell short to' use the wrong preposition. 'Fell shortly of' wrongly turns 'short' into the adverb 'shortly' (soon).

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The success of the merger **hinges in** the approval of the regulator.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'hinge on' (or 'hinge upon') = depend entirely on
solution.explanation: 'Hinge on' means depend entirely on. The merger's success depends on the regulator's approval: 'The success of the merger hinges on the approval of the regulator.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hinges at' and 'is hinging to' use the wrong prepositions, and the continuous form is not used for this state. 'Hinges in' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Four question tags were used at a branch counter. Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: She is coming to the meeting, isn't it?
You will sign the form today, won't you?
He hardly ever pays late, doesn't he?
Let us begin the meeting, won't we?

solution.concept: Question tags: same auxiliary and pronoun as the statement, with the opposite polarity
solution.explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag with the same auxiliary and a matching pronoun: 'You will ..., won't you?'
steps: A: 'She is ...' → tag 'isn't she?', not 'isn't it?'
C: 'hardly ever' is negative → positive tag 'does he?'
solution.why_others_wrong: A uses 'it' instead of the subject pronoun 'she'. C needs a positive tag because 'hardly' makes the statement negative. D: the tag for 'Let us' is 'shall we?'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: You will sign the form today, won't you?

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: The scissors on the counter are blunt.
A pair of new spectacles costs a lot these days.
His trousers is torn at the knee.
The goods were delivered to the warehouse on time.

solution.concept: Nouns that exist only in the plural (trousers, scissors, goods) take plural verbs; 'a pair of' takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'Trousers' is a plural-only noun, so the verb must be plural: 'His trousers are torn at the knee.'
steps: B: 'A pair ... costs': the head noun 'pair' is singular, correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are correct. In B the verb agrees with 'pair', which is singular.
solution.final_answer: Option C: His trousers is torn at the knee.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: The new system is as efficient, if not more efficient than, the old one.
The new system is as efficient as, if not more efficient, the old one.
The new system is as efficient, if not more, than the old one.
The new system is as efficient as, if not more efficient than, the old one.

solution.concept: Double comparison: each part ('as ... as' and 'more ... than') must be complete
solution.explanation: Remove the bracketed phrase and the sentence must still work, and the bracketed phrase must also be complete on its own. Only D passes both tests: 'as efficient as the old one' and 'more efficient than the old one'.
steps: Test 1 (remove 'if not ...'): 'as efficient as the old one' needs the second 'as'
Test 2: 'more efficient than the old one' needs 'than'
solution.why_others_wrong: A drops the second 'as'. B drops 'than'. C drops both the second 'as' and the adjective after 'more', leaving 'as efficient ... than'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The new system is as efficient as, if not more efficient than, the old one.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is INCORRECT because of a faulty comparison?

options.text: The Pune branch earns more than any branch of the bank.
The Pune branch earns more than any other branch of the bank.
The Pune branch earns more than any branch of the rival bank.
No other branch of the bank earns as much as the Pune branch.

solution.concept: Comparison within the same group needs 'any other'
solution.explanation: The Pune branch is itself a branch of the bank, so 'more than any branch of the bank' compares it with itself as well. Within the same group, the comparison must be 'than any other branch'.
steps: A: Pune branch is one of 'the bank's' branches → needs 'any other': incorrect
B: 'any other branch of the bank': correct
C: rival bank's branches are a different group, so 'any' is correct
D: positive-degree form 'No other ... as much as': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D are correct. C is correct without 'other' because the Pune branch does not belong to the rival bank.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The Pune branch earns more than any branch of the bank.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: Should you need any help, please call the branch.
Had the auditors not raised the alarm, the fraud would have gone unnoticed.
Did the bank know the borrower's history, it would have refused the loan.
Were the rupee to weaken further, imports would become costlier.

solution.concept: Inverted conditionals are formed only with 'should', 'had' and 'were', never with 'did'
solution.explanation: A conditional can drop 'if' and invert only with 'should', 'had' or 'were'. 'Did the bank know ...' cannot replace 'If the bank had known ...'. Correct: 'Had the bank known the borrower's history, it would have refused the loan.'
steps: A: 'Should you need ...' = If you need: correct
B: 'Had the auditors not raised ...': correct
C: 'Did the bank know ...': not a possible inversion; incorrect
D: 'Were the rupee to weaken ...': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D use the three accepted inversions (should, had, were) correctly.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Did the bank know the borrower's history, it would have refused the loan.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) The next morning, he took the bag to the bank and handed it to the manager.
(B) While locking up his shop one evening, Ravi noticed a cloth bag lying near the steps.
(C) Inside it he found a passbook and a bundle of cash.
(D) The manager traced the owner, an old farmer, who had dropped it on his way home.
(E) Since the bank had already closed for the day, he kept the bag safely overnight.

solution.concept: Para jumble: named opener, then discovery, decision, action and outcome
solution.explanation: B introduces Ravi and the bag. C ('Inside it') opens the bag and finds a passbook, which links it to the bank. E explains why he waited ('the bank had already closed'). A follows with 'The next morning'. D, the manager tracing the owner, comes last.
steps: Opener: B (names Ravi; others use 'he' or 'it')
C → E: the passbook points to the bank, which is closed
E → A ('The next morning') → D: BCEAD
solution.why_others_wrong: BCADE has the bank closing after he has already handed the bag over. BACED takes the bag to the bank before he knows what is inside. CBEAD opens with 'Inside it' before any bag is mentioned.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Last month, the bank introduced a token system at its busiest branch.
(P) Each customer now collects a numbered token at the entrance.
(Q) When the number is displayed on a screen, the customer goes to the counter shown beside it.
(R) Until then, he can sit and wait instead of standing in a queue.
(S) Customers say the new system has made their visits far less tiring.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; process order and the time reference 'Until then'
solution.explanation: P describes the first step (collecting a token). Q describes when the customer goes to the counter. R ('Until then') refers back to Q's moment, the number being displayed. S gives the customers' verdict.
steps: (1) → P: first step of the new system
P → Q: what happens to the token number
Q → R: 'Until then' = until the number is displayed
solution.why_others_wrong: PRQS puts 'Until then' before any moment has been mentioned. QPRS describes the number being displayed before customers collect tokens. PQSR gives the verdict before finishing the description.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) He decided to stay ashore and persuaded his neighbours to do the same.
(B) By noon, the storm had struck the coast with great force.
(C) Murugan, a fisherman, had always set out to sea before dawn.
(D) Several boats from other villages, whose crews had not received the warning, were badly damaged.
(E) One morning, however, a message on his phone warned of a sudden storm.

solution.concept: Para jumble: habit → change ('however') → decision → event → consequence
solution.explanation: C introduces Murugan and his habit. E ('One morning, however') breaks the habit with a warning. A gives his decision. B ('By noon') reports the storm, and D contrasts the fate of crews who had no warning.
steps: C → E: 'however' contrasts with his usual habit
E → A: his response to the warning
solution.why_others_wrong: CAEBD has him stay ashore before any warning arrives. ECABD opens with 'his phone' before Murugan is named. CEBAD has the storm strike before he decides to stay ashore.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Many patients, however, distrust them, assuming that a lower price means lower quality.
(B) If that trust is built, families could save a large share of what they spend on medicines.
(C) Generic medicines contain the same active ingredients as branded ones but are sold under their chemical names.
(D) Because they do not carry the cost of advertising, they are often far cheaper.
(E) Doctors and pharmacists can help overcome this doubt by explaining that generics must meet the same quality standards.

solution.concept: Para jumble: definition → advantage → objection ('however') → remedy → result
solution.explanation: C defines generic medicines. D gives their advantage (cheaper). A ('however') raises the patients' doubt about a low price. E offers the remedy for 'this doubt'. B ('If that trust is built') states the result.
steps: C → D: 'they' = generics; why they are cheaper
A → E ('this doubt') → B ('that trust'): CDAEB
solution.why_others_wrong: CADEB raises distrust of a low price before the low price is mentioned. DCAEB opens with 'they' before generics are introduced. CDEAB mentions 'this doubt' before the doubt is described.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Television news in India is now often accompanied by a sign-language interpreter in a corner of the screen.
(P) This shortage is the main reason why many channels still offer no interpretation at all.
(Q) For millions of people with hearing loss, that small window is the only way to follow the news as it happens.
(R) Expanding training courses would therefore benefit not only viewers but also schools, hospitals and courts.
(S) Trained interpreters, however, remain scarce, and the few who exist are in heavy demand.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; demonstratives ('that small window', 'This shortage') and 'therefore' as links
solution.explanation: Q explains why the interpreter's window in (1) matters. S ('however') introduces the scarcity of interpreters. P ('This shortage') refers to S. R ('therefore') draws the conclusion: train more interpreters.
steps: (1) → Q: 'that small window' = the interpreter's corner
S → P: 'This shortage' refers to S
solution.why_others_wrong: QPSR mentions 'This shortage' before any shortage is stated. SPQR uses 'however' with nothing to contrast and moves the window's importance after the shortage. QSRP draws the conclusion before P completes the problem.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Bananas meant for distant markets are therefore harvested while still green and hard.
(B) A ripe banana bruises easily and spoils within a few days.
(C) Near the market, they are placed in ripening rooms where a small dose of ethylene gas starts the process evenly.
(D) This gas is produced naturally by the fruit itself, so the method adds nothing foreign to it.
(E) The fruit that reaches the shop is thus ripe, unbruised and ready to eat.

solution.concept: Para jumble: problem → solution ('therefore') → next step → explanation → result ('thus')
solution.explanation: B states the problem (ripe bananas spoil). A ('therefore') gives the solution: pick them green. C describes ripening near the market. D ('This gas') explains C's ethylene. E ('thus') states the result.
steps: B → A: 'therefore' follows from the problem
solution.why_others_wrong: BCADE ripens the bananas before they are harvested. ABCDE opens with 'therefore' with nothing before it. BACED separates 'This gas' (D) from the gas it refers to in C.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Thousands of palm-leaf manuscripts lie in temples, monasteries and private homes across India.
(P) Besides helping distant scholars, this means the fragile originals need to be handled far less often.
(Q) Digitisation projects now photograph each leaf at high resolution before it is too late.
(R) Many of them are crumbling because of heat, humidity and insects.
(S) The images are then stored online, where scholars anywhere can study them.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; problem, response, next step ('then') and added benefit ('Besides')
solution.explanation: R describes the manuscripts' decay ('Many of them'). Q gives the response ('before it is too late'). S ('then') is the next step: storing the images online for scholars. P ('Besides helping distant scholars') adds a second benefit, so it must follow S.
steps: R → Q: 'before it is too late' answers the decay
S → P: 'Besides helping distant scholars' refers to S: RQSP
solution.why_others_wrong: RSQP mentions 'The images' before any photographs are taken. QRSP puts the urgency ('too late') before the decay that explains it. RQPS refers to 'helping distant scholars' before scholars are mentioned.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) These are small warehouses, closed to walk-in shoppers, from which riders collect orders.
(B) Quick-commerce apps promise to deliver groceries within minutes of an order.
(C) To keep that promise, they rely on a network of so-called dark stores.
(D) Critics, however, worry about the pressure such tight deadlines place on riders on busy roads.
(E) Because each store serves only a few square kilometres, a rider rarely has far to travel.

solution.concept: Para jumble: claim → method → definition → how it works → criticism
solution.explanation: B states the promise. C ('that promise') introduces dark stores. A ('These are') defines them. E explains why delivery is quick. D ('however') raises the critics' concern about deadlines.
steps: A → E (how they speed delivery) → D (criticism): BCAED
solution.why_others_wrong: BACED uses 'These' before dark stores are named. CBAED opens with 'that promise' before the promise is made. BCDAE puts the criticism between the term and its definition, so 'These' would wrongly point to the critics' deadlines.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) In some villages, the panchayat now paints its annual budget on a wall in the main square.
(P) Residents have begun to ask why a drain listed as complete has not been built.
(Q) Transparency, it seems, works best when information is placed where people already gather.
(R) Anyone passing by can see how much was allotted for roads, drains and the school.
(S) Such questions were rare when the figures were kept in a register in the panchayat office.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; effect, contrast with the past ('Such questions') and general conclusion
solution.explanation: R explains what the painted budget shows. P describes the result: residents ask questions. S ('Such questions') refers to P and contrasts with the past. Q draws the general lesson.
steps: (1) → R: what the wall shows passers-by
R → P: residents use that information to ask questions
P → S: 'Such questions' refers to P
solution.why_others_wrong: RSPQ uses 'Such questions' before any question is asked. PRSQ has residents asking about the drain before the figures are described. RPQS draws the conclusion before S completes the contrast.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Evidence from the market for investment products suggests otherwise.
(B) Their money stays in a savings account, earning less than it could, not because they prefer it there but because deciding feels too hard.
(C) It might seem that more choice must always leave consumers better off.
(D) Simplifying the menu, by offering a few clearly explained products, may therefore help more people than adding yet another scheme.
(E) Faced with dozens of almost identical mutual fund schemes, many first-time investors simply do nothing.

solution.concept: Para jumble: common belief → 'suggests otherwise' → evidence → its consequence → conclusion ('therefore')
solution.explanation: C states the common belief. A ('suggests otherwise') challenges it. E gives the evidence. B ('Their money') describes what happens to those investors. D ('therefore') draws the conclusion.
steps: Opener: C (the belief to be challenged)
C → A: 'otherwise' needs a claim before it
E → B ('Their' = first-time investors) → D ('therefore'): CAEBD
solution.why_others_wrong: CEABD gives the evidence before saying it contradicts anything, leaving 'otherwise' after the evidence. ACEBD opens with 'otherwise' with nothing to contradict. CAEDB draws the conclusion before B finishes the evidence, leaving 'Their money' without a clear referent.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Antibiotics are among the most valuable medicines ever discovered.
(P) If this continues, infections that are easily treated today could once again become deadly.
(Q) Each such useless dose gives bacteria another chance to develop resistance.
(R) A cold, for instance, is caused by a virus, against which an antibiotic is useless.
(S) Their very success, however, has encouraged careless use, from self-medication for common colds to routine use on poultry farms.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'however', 'for instance', 'such' and 'this' as links
solution.explanation: S ('Their very success, however') turns from (1)'s praise to careless use. R ('for instance') explains why using antibiotics for colds is useless. Q ('Each such useless dose') refers to R. P ('If this continues') gives the danger.
steps: S → R: 'for instance' expands the colds example
R → Q: 'such useless dose' refers to R's 'useless'
solution.why_others_wrong: SQRP says 'such useless dose' before R explains why the dose is useless. RSQP opens with an example before the careless use it illustrates. SRPQ warns 'If this continues' before Q states the mechanism.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Loading a single ship could take a week, and theft and damage were common.
(B) Because every container has the same dimensions, cranes, trucks and trains everywhere can handle it without unpacking the goods inside.
(C) The standard steel container changed all this.
(D) Until the middle of the twentieth century, cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece, in sacks, barrels and crates.
(E) The resulting fall in shipping costs is one reason why a shirt sold in one country is so often made in another.

solution.concept: Para jumble: old situation → its problems → turning point ('all this') → how it works → result
solution.explanation: D describes the old method. A adds its problems. C ('changed all this') refers to D and A. B explains how the container works. E ('The resulting fall') states the result of B.
steps: D → A: problems of loading piece by piece
A → C: 'all this' = the old method and its problems
solution.why_others_wrong: DCABE says the container 'changed all this' before the problems are described. ADCBE begins with a ship's loading time before the old method is introduced. DACEB states the result before explaining how the container works.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) a new ATM
(Q) has installed
(R) the bank
(S) near the bus stand

solution.concept: Subject + verb + object + place
solution.explanation: 'The bank has installed a new ATM near the bus stand.' The subject (R) comes first, then the verb (Q), the object (P) and the place (S).
solution.why_others_wrong: PQRS would make the ATM install the bank. RPQS puts the object between the subject and the verb. QRPS starts with the verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) which had been pending for months
(Q) was finally approved
(R) the farmers' request for a new branch
(S) after the minister's visit

solution.concept: Noun + relative clause before the main verb; time phrase last
solution.explanation: 'The farmers' request for a new branch, which had been pending for months, was finally approved after the minister's visit.' The relative clause (P) must follow 'request' (R), and the main verb (Q) follows the whole subject.
steps: Main verb: Q; time: S: RPQS
solution.why_others_wrong: RQPS separates 'which' from 'request' so that it seems to refer to the approval. PRQS opens with 'which'. RPSQ puts the time phrase between the subject and its verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) that the board had no choice
(Q) seek fresh capital from the government
(R) so heavy were the losses
(S) but to

solution.concept: Inverted 'So + adjective + verb + subject ... that'; 'no choice but to + verb'
solution.explanation: 'So heavy were the losses that the board had no choice but to seek fresh capital from the government.' R opens with the inverted 'So ... were the losses', P gives the result clause, and 'no choice' is completed by 'but to' (S) and the verb phrase (Q).
steps: Opener: R ('So heavy were the losses')
Result clause: P ('that the board had no choice')
'no choice but to' + verb: S then Q: RPSQ
solution.why_others_wrong: RSPQ and RPQS break the fixed phrase 'no choice but to seek'. PRSQ opens with 'that', leaving the 'So' clause in the middle.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The customer was ______ when the cashier returned the extra money she had paid by mistake.

solution.concept: Single blank: the reaction to a kind act
solution.explanation: The cashier honestly returned money paid by mistake. The natural reaction is thankfulness: she was 'grateful'.
steps: Reaction to an honest favour: thankful
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Annoyed' does not fit a helpful act. 'Careless' and 'absent' do not describe a reaction to what happened.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The bank will ______ a penalty if the borrower misses three instalments in a row.

solution.concept: Confusable words: impose (enforce a charge or rule) vs oppose, propose, expose
solution.explanation: A bank enforces a penalty on a borrower who misses payments: it 'imposes' a penalty.
steps: Collocation: impose a penalty / fine / tax
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Oppose' (resist), 'propose' (suggest) and 'expose' (reveal) do not describe enforcing a charge.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The branch was ______ for repairs, so customers were ______ to the branch across the road.

solution.concept: Double blank: cause and result joined by 'so'
solution.explanation: Repairs mean the branch was closed, so customers were sent (directed) to another branch.
steps: Blank 1: a branch under repair is 'closed'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Opened ... for repairs' does not explain why customers went elsewhere. 'Prevented to' is not the right pattern ('prevented from'). 'Crowded ... invited' breaks the cause and result.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The new manager is easy to ______; within a week, the whole staff liked him.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: get along with = have a friendly relationship with
solution.explanation: The staff liked him within a week, so he was easy to have a friendly relationship with: 'easy to get along with'.
steps: Meaning needed: be on good terms with
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Get away with' means escape punishment. 'Get over with' means finish something unpleasant. 'Get through with' means complete a task. None describes a friendly relationship.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The merger talks reached a ______ when neither bank would agree on who should lead the combined entity.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'neither ... would agree' signals a standstill
solution.explanation: When neither side will give way, talks cannot move forward: they reach a deadlock.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Consensus' (agreement) is the opposite. 'Milestone' suggests progress. 'Reached a conclusion' would mean the talks were settled, which contradicts the disagreement.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The scheme was ______ in theory, but poor ______ meant that few farmers ever benefited from it.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'in theory ... but' contrasts design with execution
solution.explanation: 'In theory ... but' sets good design against bad execution: the scheme was sound in theory, but poor implementation kept the benefits from reaching farmers.
steps: Blank 1: positive, because 'but' introduces a problem → 'sound'
solution.why_others_wrong: A: 'flawed in theory' removes the contrast with 'but'. C: 'poor intentions' contradicts a scheme that was sound. D: 'poor weather' does not contrast with 'in theory', and 'popular in theory' is odd.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
With costs rising and deposits falling, the bank had no choice but to ______ its plans for rural expansion.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: scale back = reduce in size or extent
solution.explanation: Rising costs and falling deposits force a bank to cut its plans: it must 'scale back' its expansion.
steps: 'had no choice but to' → an unwelcome cut
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Scale up' (enlarge) contradicts the pressure. 'Back up' (support) and 'draw up' (prepare a plan) do not express a forced reduction.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The bank's accounts were so ______ that even the auditors could not tell where the money had gone.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'so ... that' result
solution.explanation: The result is that even auditors could not trace the money, so the accounts must have been hard to understand: 'opaque' (not transparent, unclear).
steps: Result: auditors could not trace the money
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lucid' (clear), 'meticulous' (very careful) and 'prudent' (sensible) would make the money easier to trace, not harder.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
His ______ stance in the negotiations, refusing to concede even minor points, eventually drove the investors away.

solution.concept: Single blank: the participle phrase defines the blank
solution.explanation: 'Refusing to concede even minor points' describes someone who will not compromise: 'intransigent'.
steps: Definition clue: 'refusing to concede even minor points'
Result 'drove the investors away' confirms a negative quality
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Accommodating' and 'pliant' mean willing to adjust, the opposite. 'Genial' (friendly) does not describe refusing to concede.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
Instead of ______ the crisis, the hasty measures only ______ public panic, and depositors queued outside branches the next morning.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'Instead of' contrasts the intended effect with the actual one
solution.explanation: The measures were meant to calm the crisis but did the opposite, as the queues show. 'Instead of defusing the crisis, the hasty measures only fuelled public panic.'
steps: Result clue: depositors queued the next morning → panic grew
Blank 1: the opposite, the intended effect → 'defusing'
solution.why_others_wrong: B reverses both words and contradicts the queues. C ('eased panic') contradicts the queues and removes the contrast. D ('prevented panic') also contradicts the queues.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The bank's new chairman has promised to ______ the culture of aggressive sales targets that led to mis-selling.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: root out = find and remove completely
solution.explanation: A culture that led to mis-selling is something to be eliminated. 'Root out' means find and remove completely.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Root for' means support or cheer on. 'Bring about' (cause to happen) and 'set up' (establish) would create the culture, not end it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) receipt** counted the **(B) notes** twice before handing them to the **(C) customer**, who signed the **(D) teller**.

solution.concept: Word swap: check who can perform each action
solution.explanation: A receipt cannot count notes, and a customer does not sign a teller. Swapping A and D gives: 'The teller counted the notes twice before handing them to the customer, who signed the receipt.'
steps: 'The receipt counted' is meaningless → A is misplaced
'signed the teller' is meaningless → D is misplaced
solution.why_others_wrong: A-B gives 'The notes counted the receipt'. B-C gives 'counted the customer twice before handing them to the notes'. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'proscribe' used correctly?

options.text: The doctor proscribed rest and plenty of fluids for a week.
Students must read the proscribed textbooks before the examination.
The law proscribes the sale of tobacco products to minors.
The bank has proscribed a new format for loan applications.

solution.concept: Proscribe (forbid, ban) vs prescribe (recommend, lay down as a rule)
solution.explanation: 'Proscribe' means forbid by law. 'The law proscribes the sale of tobacco products to minors' means the law bans it, which is correct.
steps: B: textbooks laid down for a course → 'prescribed'
C: the law forbids a sale → 'proscribes': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D all need 'prescribe', meaning recommend or lay down; using 'proscribe' would mean the rest, textbooks and format were banned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The law proscribes the sale of tobacco products to minors.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'dormant' as used in the sentence:
'The bank wrote to her about her dormant account, which had seen no transactions for over two years.'

solution.concept: Dormant = inactive, not in use for a period
solution.explanation: The sentence explains the word: the account 'had seen no transactions for over two years'. A dormant account is an inactive one.
steps: Clue: no transactions for over two years
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Overdrawn' (more taken out than deposited), 'jointly held' and 'newly opened' all describe something other than a lack of activity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'stringent' as used in the sentence:
'After a string of defaults, the regulator introduced stringent norms for lending to property developers.'

solution.concept: Stringent = strict, severe
solution.explanation: A regulator reacting to a string of defaults tightens the rules: 'stringent norms' are strict ones.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lenient' is the opposite. 'Vague' and 'temporary' do not describe a tougher response to defaults.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Advanced vocabulary: synonym and antonym pairs
solution.explanation: 'Ephemeral' and 'transient' both mean lasting only a short time. The other three pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and D are pairs of opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Advanced vocabulary: synonym and antonym pairs
solution.explanation: 'Laconic' means using very few words; 'verbose' means using too many. They are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are pairs of synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'sanguine' as used in the sentence:
'Despite the slowdown, the chairman remained sanguine about the bank's prospects for the coming year.'

solution.concept: Sanguine = cheerfully hopeful, optimistic
solution.explanation: 'Despite the slowdown' sets up a contrast: the economy is weak, yet the chairman stays hopeful. 'Sanguine' means optimistic.
steps: 'Despite' signals an attitude that runs against the bad news
Hopeful in spite of a slowdown
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Gloomy' is the opposite and removes the contrast with 'Despite'. 'Indifferent' and 'secretive' do not describe a view of the bank's prospects.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The bank will **commence** its annual audit next Monday.

solution.concept: Commence = begin
solution.explanation: To 'commence' something is to begin it; the audit will begin next Monday.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Postpone' and 'cancel' mean the audit will not start then. 'Complete' refers to the end, not the start.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Clean drinking water is **vital** for the health of the village.

solution.concept: Vital = absolutely necessary
solution.explanation: Clean water is absolutely necessary for health. 'Vital' means essential.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Harmful' and 'optional' contradict the meaning. 'Costly' describes price, not necessity.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The inspector will **scrutinise** every loan file before the audit report is finalised.

solution.concept: Scrutinise = examine closely and thoroughly
solution.explanation: Before a report is finalised, an inspector checks each file carefully. 'Scrutinise' means examine closely.
steps: Context: checking before finalising a report
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Approve' and 'sign' are actions after checking, not the checking itself. 'Ignore' is the opposite.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Updating KYC details online will **obviate** the need for most customers to visit the branch.

solution.concept: Obviate = remove (a need or difficulty), make unnecessary
solution.explanation: If KYC can be updated online, customers no longer need to visit the branch. 'Obviate the need' means remove the need.
steps: Context: online updating replaces a branch visit
So the need for a visit disappears
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Create' is the opposite. 'Highlight' and 'delay' the need do not fit the effect of an online option.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The bank offers **temporary** jobs to students during the festive season.

solution.concept: Temporary = lasting for a limited time; antonym: permanent
solution.explanation: A 'temporary' job lasts only for a limited period. The opposite is 'permanent'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Short', 'seasonal' and 'brief' are all close in meaning to 'temporary'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The company plans to **expand** its operations in rural areas next year.

solution.concept: Expand = make larger; antonym: reduce
solution.explanation: To 'expand' operations is to enlarge them. The opposite is to 'reduce' them.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Grow', 'extend' and 'widen' are all similar in meaning to 'expand'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The cashier quickly identified the five-hundred-rupee note as **genuine**.

solution.concept: Genuine = real, not fake; antonym: counterfeit
solution.explanation: A 'genuine' note is real. The opposite is a 'counterfeit' (fake) note.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Authentic', 'real' and 'valid' are all similar in meaning to 'genuine'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The witness gave a **candid** account of what had happened at the counter.

solution.concept: Candid = frank and truthful; antonym: evasive
solution.explanation: A 'candid' account is frank and holds nothing back. The opposite is an 'evasive' account, one that avoids giving direct answers.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Frank', 'honest' and 'open' are all similar in meaning to 'candid'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The fresh capital is expected to **augment** the bank's lending capacity.

solution.concept: Augment = increase; antonym: diminish
solution.explanation: To 'augment' is to make larger or add to. The opposite is to 'diminish', to make smaller.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Increase', 'boost' and 'strengthen' are all similar in meaning to 'augment'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'the tip of the iceberg'.

options.text: a small, visible part of a much larger problem
the most dangerous part of a journey
the final stage of a task

solution.concept: Idiom: the tip of the iceberg
solution.explanation: Only a small part of an iceberg shows above the water. The idiom means a small, visible part of a much bigger problem. For example: 'The frauds detected so far may be just the tip of the iceberg.'
steps: Image: most of an iceberg is hidden under water
Meaning: a small visible part of a larger problem
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D take one word of the image ('tip' or 'ice') literally and have no link with the idiom's meaning.
solution.final_answer: Option A: a small, visible part of a much larger problem

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
The security guard was dismissed for **turning a blind eye** to the thefts from the staff lockers.

solution.concept: Idiom: turn a blind eye (to) = pretend not to notice
solution.explanation: The guard was dismissed because he knew about the thefts but deliberately ignored them.
steps: Context: a guard dismissed over thefts
Idiom: pretend not to see something wrong
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Reporting promptly' and 'investigating carefully' would not lead to dismissal. 'Being unable to see clearly' takes the idiom literally.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
The new flyover, built at great cost but hardly used by anyone, has become a **white elephant**.

options.text: a project that is completed ahead of time
a costly possession that is of little use

solution.concept: Idiom: white elephant = something costly to build or keep but of little use
solution.explanation: The flyover cost a great deal but is hardly used: it is a costly thing of little use, a 'white elephant'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A symbol of national pride' and 'a rare and beautiful object' miss the idea of uselessness. 'Completed ahead of time' has no link with the idiom.
solution.final_answer: Option D: a costly possession that is of little use

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to be in the red'.

options.text: to be in debt or making a loss
to be in danger of an accident

solution.concept: Idiom: in the red = owing money, making a loss (from losses once written in red ink)
solution.explanation: A business that is 'in the red' is losing money or is in debt. Its opposite is 'in the black'.
steps: Origin: losses were entered in red ink
Meaning: in debt, making a loss
solution.why_others_wrong: A and D link red with anger or embarrassment, and C with danger, but the idiom refers only to finances.
solution.final_answer: Option B: to be in debt or making a loss

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Stop **beating about the bush** and tell us plainly whether the loan has been approved.

solution.concept: Idiom: beat about (or around) the bush = avoid coming to the point
solution.explanation: The speaker wants a plain answer, so the listener has been avoiding the main point.
steps: So the person has been talking around the point
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Working very hard', 'making a loud noise' and 'wasting money' do not contrast with telling something plainly.
solution.final_answer: Option A: avoiding the main point

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Everyone agreed that the regional head's bullying should be reported, but nobody was willing to **bell the cat**.

options.text: take the risk of confronting a powerful person

solution.concept: Idiom: bell the cat = take on a dangerous task on behalf of a group
solution.explanation: Everyone wanted the bullying reported, but reporting a powerful boss is risky. Nobody would take that risk: nobody would 'bell the cat'.
steps: Context: all agree on an action against a powerful person
'but nobody was willing' → the action is risky
Idiom: take the risky step for the group
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Share the credit' and 'make a hasty decision' do not fit. 'Keep a secret' is the opposite of reporting.
solution.final_answer: Option C: take the risk of confronting a powerful person

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the phrase in bold.
The bank won the long court case, but it was a **Pyrrhic victory**: the legal costs were greater than the amount it recovered.

options.text: a victory that brings fame but no money
a victory won at so great a cost that it is hardly worth winning

solution.concept: Phrase: Pyrrhic victory = a win that costs the winner almost as much as, or more than, a defeat
solution.explanation: The explanation after the colon makes the meaning clear: the bank spent more on legal costs than it recovered, so the win was not worth its cost.
steps: Explanation after the colon: costs exceeded the gain
A win not worth its price = Pyrrhic victory
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing suggests cheating (A) or an easy win (B). C is wrong because the problem is the cost, not a lack of money from fame.
solution.final_answer: Option D: a victory won at so great a cost that it is hardly worth winning

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A temporary suspension of an activity or of an obligation, such as the repayment of loans

solution.concept: One-word substitution: finance and law terms
solution.explanation: A 'moratorium' is a temporary suspension of an activity or obligation, for example a moratorium on loan repayments.
steps: Key ideas: temporary + suspension of an obligation
solution.why_others_wrong: An 'embargo' is an official ban, usually on trade. A 'sanction' is a penalty or an official permission. An 'amnesty' is an official pardon.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
The dishonest taking of money that has been placed in one's care

solution.concept: One-word substitution: financial wrongdoing
solution.explanation: 'Embezzlement' is the theft of money by someone who has been trusted to look after it, such as an employee or official.
steps: Key ideas: money entrusted to the person + dishonestly taken
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Extortion' is obtaining money by threats. 'Bribery' is offering money to influence someone. 'Forgery' is making a false copy of a document or signature.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A position that requires little or no work but gives the holder a salary or status

solution.concept: One-word substitution: positions and payments
solution.explanation: A 'sinecure' is a post that brings pay or status without real duties.
steps: Key ideas: little or no work + salary or status
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Tenure' is the period for which a post is held. A 'stipend' is a fixed allowance, such as an apprentice's pay. A 'prerogative' is a special right or privilege.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The clerk is counting the cash.

options.text: The cash is counted by the clerk.
The cash was being counted by the clerk.
The cash is being counted by the clerk.
The cash has been counted by the clerk.

solution.concept: Present continuous active → is/are being + past participle
solution.explanation: 'Is counting' becomes 'is being counted'; the object 'the cash' becomes the subject and 'the clerk' the agent.
solution.why_others_wrong: A changes the tense to present simple. B changes it to past continuous. D changes it to present perfect.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The cash is being counted by the clerk.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
People say that the bank is planning a merger.

options.text: The bank is said to plan a merger.
The bank was said to be planning a merger.
It is said that the bank was planning a merger.
The bank is said to be planning a merger.

solution.concept: Passive of reporting verbs: subject + is said + to be + -ing for an action in progress
solution.explanation: 'People say that the bank is planning ...' becomes 'The bank is said to be planning a merger.' The present 'is said' matches 'say', and the continuous infinitive 'to be planning' matches 'is planning'.
steps: Subject of the 'that' clause → subject of the sentence
solution.why_others_wrong: A uses the simple infinitive 'to plan', which loses the sense of an action in progress. B changes 'say' to the past 'was said'. C wrongly changes 'is planning' to 'was planning'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The bank is said to be planning a merger.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
He asked me, "Where do you work?"

options.text: He asked me where did I work.
He asked me where I worked.
He asked me where do I work.
He asked me that where I worked.

solution.concept: Wh-question in reported speech: statement word order + backshift, no 'that'
solution.explanation: A reported wh-question keeps the question word, uses statement order (subject before verb) and moves the tense back: 'He asked me where I worked.'
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C keep question order ('did I work', 'do I work'). D adds 'that' before the question word.
solution.final_answer: Option B: He asked me where I worked.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
The manager said, "What a careful worker she is!"

options.text: The manager exclaimed that she was a very careful worker.
The manager said what a careful worker was she.
The manager exclaimed that what a careful worker she is.
The manager asked what a careful worker she was.

solution.concept: Exclamatory sentence in reported speech: 'exclaimed that' + statement form + backshift
solution.explanation: An exclamation is reported with a verb such as 'exclaimed', and the exclamation becomes a statement: 'What a careful worker she is!' → 'that she was a very careful worker'.
solution.why_others_wrong: B inverts the verb ('was she') as if it were a question. C keeps 'what' after 'that' and does not backshift. D uses 'asked', but the original is an exclamation, not a question.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The manager exclaimed that she was a very careful worker.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Ten kilometres ______ a long distance to walk to the nearest bank branch.

solution.concept: A plural amount of distance, money or time seen as one quantity takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'Ten kilometres' is treated here as a single distance, not ten separate kilometres, so the verb is singular: 'Ten kilometres is a long distance.'
steps: Is the subject one amount or separate items? One distance
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are', 'were' and 'have been' are plural and treat the distance as separate kilometres, against the singular complement 'a long distance'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Opening new branches in remote hill districts ______ proved far more expensive than the bank expected.

solution.concept: A gerund phrase used as the subject is singular, whatever plural noun it contains
solution.explanation: The subject is the activity 'Opening new branches ...', a gerund phrase, which takes a singular verb. 'Branches' is only the object of 'opening'. So: 'Opening new branches ... has proved far more expensive.'
steps: Subject: the gerund phrase 'Opening new branches in remote hill districts'
A gerund subject is singular ('branches' is the object of 'opening')
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Have' wrongly agrees with 'branches'. 'Are proved' and 'were proved' are plural passive forms that also change the meaning to 'were shown to be'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
None of the stolen money ______ been recovered so far.

solution.concept: 'None of' + uncountable noun takes a singular verb
solution.explanation: 'Money' is uncountable, so 'none of the stolen money' is singular: 'None of the stolen money has been recovered.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Have' and 'were' are plural forms. 'Are been' is ungrammatical. An uncountable noun after 'none of' takes a singular verb.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
Two-thirds of the farmland in the district ______ irrigated by canals.

solution.concept: Fractions and percentages agree with the noun after 'of'
solution.explanation: With a fraction, the verb agrees with the noun that follows 'of'. 'Farmland' is uncountable and singular, so the verb is singular: 'Two-thirds of the farmland is irrigated.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are' and 'were' wrongly agree with the plural-looking 'two-thirds'. 'Have irrigated' would make the farmland the doer of the irrigation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
While the clerk ______ the cash, the power suddenly went off.

solution.concept: Past continuous for an action in progress interrupted by a short past event
solution.explanation: The counting was in progress when the power failure (a sudden, short event) happened. The longer background action takes the past continuous: 'While the clerk was counting the cash, the power went off.'
steps: Short event: 'the power suddenly went off' (simple past)
Background action in progress at that moment
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Counted' and 'had counted' present the counting as completed, which clashes with 'While'. 'Is counting' is present and does not match 'went off'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
If he had accepted the transfer last year, he ______ a branch manager now.

solution.concept: Mixed conditional: past condition (had + V3) with a present result (would + base verb)
solution.explanation: The condition is past ('had accepted ... last year') but the result is about the present ('now'). This mixed conditional uses 'would be' in the result clause: 'he would be a branch manager now'.
steps: Condition: past perfect ('had accepted last year')
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Would have been' refers to the past and clashes with 'now'. 'Will be' is used for real future conditions. 'Had been' cannot stand in the result clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
This is the third time this month that the bank's server ______ down.

solution.concept: 'This is the first/second/third time (that) ...' takes the present perfect
solution.explanation: After 'This is the third time that ...', the clause counts experiences up to now and takes the present perfect: 'the server has gone down'.
steps: Pattern: This is the [ordinal] time that ...
Experience counted up to now → present perfect
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Went' (simple past) and 'goes' (simple present) do not follow this pattern. 'Had gone' is past perfect and needs a past reference point, which clashes with 'This is'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Her son has ______ MBA from ______ university in Pune.

solution.concept: 'A' or 'an' depends on the first sound, not the first letter
solution.explanation: 'MBA' is read 'em-bee-ay' and begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'. 'University' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound, so it takes 'a'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A reverses the two articles. B uses 'an' before 'university'. D uses 'a' before 'MBA'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
The members elected her ______ chairperson of the cooperative bank.

solution.concept: No article before a title held by one person, used as a complement after 'elect', 'appoint' or 'make'
solution.explanation: When a unique post is the complement of 'elect', 'appoint' or 'make', it takes no article: 'They elected her chairperson.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A' and 'an' would suggest one of several chairpersons. 'An' is also wrong before the consonant sound of 'chairperson'. 'The' is not used before a title in this position.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Most of ______ lunch that we were served at ______ staff canteen yesterday was cold.

solution.concept: Meals normally take no article, but take 'the' when a particular meal is specified
solution.explanation: 'Lunch' in general takes no article ('We had lunch'). Here a relative clause ('that we were served ... yesterday') picks out one particular lunch, so it takes 'the'; 'most of' also needs a determiner before a noun. 'Staff canteen' is a particular canteen known to the speakers, so it also takes 'the'.
steps: Blank 1: a specific meal, defined by the relative clause → 'the lunch'
Blank 2: a particular, known canteen → 'the staff canteen'
solution.why_others_wrong: A applies the general no-article rule for meals although this lunch is specified. C uses 'a', which cannot follow 'Most of' and does not fit a specific, known canteen. D leaves the singular countable noun 'canteen' without any article.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
Her daughter is married ______ a doctor who works in Chennai.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'married to' someone
solution.explanation: The adjective 'married' takes 'to': 'She is married to a doctor.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Married with' is not standard for a spouse. 'Married by' names the person who conducted the ceremony. 'Married for' is used with a period of time ('married for ten years').

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The new scheme is aimed ______ helping first-time women entrepreneurs.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'aimed at' (+ noun or -ing form)
solution.explanation: 'Aim' in the sense of 'intend for a purpose' takes 'at': 'The scheme is aimed at helping first-time women entrepreneurs.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Aimed for', 'aimed to helping' and 'aimed on' are not the standard pattern; 'aimed to' would need a base verb ('aimed to help'), not 'helping'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
A stable and predictable policy environment is conducive ______ long-term investment.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'conducive to' = making something likely to happen
solution.explanation: The adjective 'conducive' takes 'to': 'conducive to long-term investment'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Conducive for', 'conducive with' and 'conducive towards' are not the standard collocation.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ it was raining heavily, all the staff reached the branch on time.

solution.concept: Contrast connector 'Although' for an unexpected result
solution.explanation: Heavy rain would normally delay people, yet everyone was on time. 'Although' introduces a fact that contrasts with the main clause.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Because' would make the rain the reason for punctuality. 'Unless' sets a condition. 'So' cannot open a clause that is joined to a following main clause like this.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
Deposits in the bank's urban branches rose by ten per cent, ______ those in its rural branches fell slightly.

solution.concept: 'Whereas' compares two contrasting facts
solution.explanation: The sentence sets two facts side by side: urban deposits rose; rural deposits fell. 'Whereas' links two contrasting statements of this kind.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Because' would make one change the cause of the other. 'So that' expresses purpose and 'unless' a condition; neither fits two facts being compared.
